a bedtime story
Bramble
and the Little Lost Star
Far away, past the farms and the fences, there is a meadow where the flowers close their petals when the sun goes down.
And under the roots of an old oak tree, in a cosy little burrow, lived a small hedgehog named Bramble.
Every evening, Bramble said goodnight to everyone. “Goodnight, flowers. Goodnight, crickets. Goodnight, sleepy moon.”
But tonight, Bramble could not fall asleep. So he sat in the clover, and looked up at the stars.
He counted them, one by one. “One… two… three… a hundred and one… a hundred and two…”
And that is when he saw it. A tiny star, tumbling out of the sky, spinning and sparkling, falling down, down, down…
…and landing — plink! — right in the middle of the clover.
Bramble tiptoed closer. There in the grass sat the smallest star he had ever seen. And she was crying.
“Hello,” said Bramble softly. “I’m Bramble. Who are you?” “I’m Pip,” sniffed the little star. “And I’m lost.”
“I was playing hide-and-seek with the other stars,” said Pip, “and I leaned out too far… and I slipped.”
“Up there is the Sleepy Bear. I’m the twinkle on the end of his nose. Without me, he can’t fall asleep.”
“And if I stay down here too long,” Pip whispered, “my light will fade away.” Her glow was already a little dimmer.
“Don’t worry, Pip,” said Bramble bravely. “I’ll help you get home.” And Pip climbed up onto his back.
But how do you get a star back into the sky? “Moon,” called Bramble, “how can we get Pip home?”
The moon gave a great big silvery yawn. “Go to the top of the tallest hill. Old Owl lives there. She can fly higher than anyone.”
So off they went. Bramble trotted through the tall, whispering grass, and Pip held on tight, glowing like a tiny lantern.
The fireflies came out to see. They blinked and they twinkled, and lit up the path ahead like a string of little lights.
Soon they came to the babbling brook. The water was cold and quick, and the stepping stones were slippery and dark.
“I can help!” said Pip, and she glowed her brightest. The stones lit up one by one, and Bramble hopped across. Hop. Hop. Hop!
On the other side, the frogs were fast asleep on their lily pads, snoring very softly. “Shhh,” said Bramble, and they tiptoed by.
Then they passed the bunny burrow, where the little rabbits were tucked up tight, dreaming of carrots and clover.
At last they reached the tallest hill. It was very steep. Bramble climbed, and climbed, and climbed, step by little step.
Halfway up, his little legs grew tired. So Pip sang him a twinkly song, and it made his feet feel light again.
And there, at the very top, in an old crooked tree, sat Old Owl, with her big round eyes and her soft brown feathers.
“Who-oo is out so late?” hooted Old Owl. “Please,” said Bramble, “Pip fell from the sky. Can you fly her home?”
“Hop on, little star,” smiled Old Owl. Pip gave Bramble the biggest, warmest hug. “Thank you, Bramble. I’ll never forget you.”
Then Old Owl spread her wings, and up, up, up they flew — past the treetops, past the clouds, all the way to the Sleepy Bear.
Pip slipped back into her place, right on the end of the bear’s nose. And the whole sky sparkled.
Down on the hill, Bramble waved and waved. And Pip twinkled back, brighter than all the other stars, just for him.
Old Owl carried Bramble home, gliding softly over the bunnies, the brook, and the snoring frogs.
Back under the old oak tree, Bramble curled up into a cosy, prickly ball. His eyes grew heavy…
Goodnight, frogs. Goodnight, bunnies. Goodnight, Old Owl. Goodnight, sleepy moon.
And goodnight, little Pip, shining on the end of the Sleepy Bear’s nose. Goodnight, Bramble. Sweet dreams.
The End
sweet dreams
Bramble and the Little Lost Star
